title: Advanced Networking: Transit Gateway, Direct Connect & Hybrid Connectivity

scenes.narration: This chapter picks up right where multi-account governance left off: now that Organizations and S C Ps decide who's allowed to do what, this chapter asks how all those accounts' networks actually reach each other. It maps to two Professional-exam domains at once — Design for New Solutions, the single largest domain at twenty nine percent, and Design Solutions for Organizational Complexity at twenty six percent. The core problem: V P C peering — the same peering you learned back at Associate level — quietly stops scaling once you pass a handful of VPCs. Transit Gateway, which you'll hear shortened to T G W, is the hub-and-spoke fix, and Direct Connect versus Site-to-Site VPN is the other half of this chapter: two genuinely different answers to how on-premises reaches AWS.

props.title: Advanced Networking: Transit Gateway, Direct Connect & Hybrid Connectivity

facts.label: The mesh problem
facts.value: VPC peering is non-transitive — full-mesh connections grow N(N−1)/2, unmanageable past a handful of VPCs

facts.label: Where this sits
facts.value: SAP-C02 · Design for New Solutions (29%) + Organizational Complexity (26%)

scenes.narration: Two instincts feel completely reasonable at small scale, and both break the same way once a scenario stops being small. First: when a new VPC shows up, just peer it to whatever it needs to reach — worked fine for two VPCs, still feels fine for three or four. Second: a scenario says 'encrypted,' and Direct Connect is a private, dedicated connection, so surely that counts. It doesn't. Private access and cryptographic encryption are two completely different guarantees, and the exam relies on candidates blurring them together.

props.heading: "Just peer it" and "Direct Connect is private, so it's secure"
bullets: Keep adding a new VPC peering connection every time a VPC needs to reach another one.
Assume a stated 'encrypted' requirement is satisfied because Direct Connect is a private, dedicated connection.
Never ask what either instinct looks like at 20, or 50, VPCs — or under a real compliance audit.

scenes.narration: Here's the fact the exam tests hardest: VPC peering is genuinely non-transitive. Peer A with B, and peer B with C, and A still cannot reach C through B — no route table setting turns that on, because a peering connection is a direct relationship between exactly two VPCs, full stop. Now scale that up. Connecting every VPC to every other VPC needs one connection per pair, and the number of pairs among N VPCs is N times N minus one, divided by two. At ten VPCs that's forty five connections. At fifty, it's twelve hundred twenty five. That's quadratic growth for a linear problem, and it's exactly what Transit Gateway exists to fix — trading that mesh for one attachment per VPC instead.

props.heading: Why A can't reach C through B — and why that never changes
steps: VPC A peers with VPC B — a direct, pairwise relationship, nothing else
VPC B peers with VPC C — a separate, independent pairwise relationship
A cannot reach C through B — peering never forwards a third VPC's traffic
Full mesh for N VPCs needs N(N−1)/2 connections — quadratic growth, not linear
50 VPCs would need 1,225 peering connections just to fully connect them all
Transit Gateway fixes this by turning N(N−1)/2 relationships into N attachments

scenes.narration: Put the two models side by side and the case makes itself. At five VPCs, a full mesh needs ten peering connections against the hub's five attachments — survivable either way. At ten VPCs, forty five against ten. By twenty VPCs it's a hundred ninety against twenty. And at fifty VPCs, the mesh needs twelve hundred twenty five separate connections to manage, while the hub still needs exactly fifty — one per VPC. That gap only gets wider as N grows, which is the entire argument for redesigning around a hub before you're forced to.

props.kicker: THE CURVE THAT FORCES THE REDESIGN
props.heading: The mesh math, side by side with the hub

scenes.narration: Step through how this actually gets built. First, create the Transit Gateway itself — a regional resource, and at this point it's just an empty router with nothing attached. Second, attach every VPC that needs cross-VPC reach as a spoke, one attachment each. Third, attach Direct Connect and Site-to-Site VPN to that same hub once, instead of wiring hybrid connectivity into every VPC individually. Fourth — the step people skip — build separate route tables, because association decides which table an attachment's traffic follows, and propagation decides which other attachments' routes show up in it. That's how production and development can share the hub while staying isolated from each other. Fifth, for a multi-region design, peer the regional Transit Gateways directly to each other, no mesh required.

props.heading: Building the hub, in the order you'd actually do it
steps: Create the Transit Gateway — one per region, empty until spokes attach
Attach each VPC as a spoke — one attachment per VPC, not one per pair
Attach Direct Connect and/or Site-to-Site VPN once, shared by every spoke
Build separate route tables — association decides membership, propagation decides visibility
Peer Transit Gateways across regions to link hubs without a mesh

scenes.narration: This is the single most exam-relevant table in the chapter, and every row is genuinely correct under the right conditions. Direct Connect is the answer when a workload needs consistent, high-throughput, low-latency hybrid connectivity and you have real lead time — commonly weeks — to provision the dedicated circuit. The catch: it doesn't encrypt anything by default, so an encryption requirement means layering a VPN session on top, or using MACsec where it's supported. Site-to-Site VPN is the answer when throughput needs are lower, the timeline is urgent, or encryption-by-default matters — it's provisioned entirely in software, live in minutes to hours, with no physical circuit to schedule, and a single tunnel's throughput ceiling can be multiplied with several tunnels and E C M P if you need more aggregate bandwidth. And Direct Connect Gateway solves a completely different problem: it lets one physical connection reach multiple VPCs and multiple regions, without touching that connection's throughput ceiling or its encryption gap at all.

props.heading: Direct Connect vs Site-to-Site VPN — the real trade

rows.label: Direct Connect
cells: Consistent high-throughput, low-latency hybrid workloads, with weeks of lead time to spare
No default encryption — pair with a VPN overlay or MACsec; a single connection is a single point of failure

rows.label: Site-to-Site VPN
cells: Lower or moderate throughput, urgent connectivity, or an encrypted-by-default requirement
Rides the public internet — throughput and latency inherit internet variability; one tunnel tops out around 1.25 Gbps

rows.label: Direct Connect Gateway
cells: One connection needs to reach multiple VPCs and/or multiple AWS Regions
Extends reach only — doesn't raise throughput or add encryption

scenes.narration: Four commands map to the whole hub-building sequence. Creating the transit gateway returns an ID everything downstream references, with nothing attached yet. Creating a VPC attachment runs once per VPC — that's the concrete command-count difference behind the mesh math you just saw. Ordering the Direct Connect connection is the step that actually starts the real-world clock: everything before it was software, and everything after involves a physical cross-connect at a colocation facility. And creating the private virtual interface — the step that B G P-peers the connection into the transit gateway — is worth studying for what it doesn't contain: there's no encryption parameter anywhere in that call, because Direct Connect was never carrying encryption to begin with.

output: # the hub — no VPCs, VPN, or Direct Connect attached yet

steps.cmd: aws ec2 create-transit-gateway-vpc-attachment --transit-gateway-id tgw-0abc123 --vpc-id vpc-0prod111 --subnet-ids subnet-0a1b2c subnet-0d3e4f
output: # one call per VPC — N VPCs means N attachments, not N(N-1)/2 connections
# this call starts the real-world clock — LOA-CFA + cross-connect scheduling follow
# note what's absent: no encryption parameter anywhere in this call

scenes.narration: Recognize this shape rather than memorize it. Transit Gateway setup is four scripts: create the hub, attach the spokes, wire up route tables, then optionally peer regions. Direct Connect is three: request the physical connection, create the private virtual interface, then optionally add a Direct Connect Gateway to fan out to more regions. And VPN backup is one script, because there's no physical provisioning step to break into pieces — it's the entire reason VPN can move this fast.

Take a concrete case. A retail chain let business units spin up VPCs for three years — they're now at forty VPCs across a dozen accounts, connected by roughly ninety hand-built peering connections, and nobody's fully confident which VPC can reach which other one. A new fraud-detection service needs to read from a dozen of those VPCs, and the mandate is to minimize new peering connections while staying manageable for a small platform team. Run it through the framework: this is exactly the migrate-to-a-hub scenario. Attach the VPCs that actually need cross-VPC reach to a Transit Gateway as spokes, retire the peering connections that replaces, and use TGW route tables — not more peering — to control exactly which spokes can see the fraud-detection VPC going forward.

scenes.narration: Try these before we reveal the answers. First: Alpha is peered with Beta, and Beta is peered with Gamma — can Alpha reach Gamma through that chain? Second, and this is the trap that catches even experienced engineers: a team is leaning on Direct Connect alone to satisfy an 'encrypted in transit' compliance requirement. Does that actually hold up?

questions.prompt: VPC Alpha is peered with VPC Beta, and VPC Beta is peered with VPC Gamma. Can an instance in Alpha reach an instance in Gamma through these two connections?
options: Yes — Beta forwards Alpha's traffic through to Gamma
No — the connections are non-transitive, and no configuration option changes that
Yes, but only if IPv6 is enabled on both connections
It depends on whether Beta's route table has a route to Gamma

questions.prompt: A team is relying on a Direct Connect connection to satisfy a compliance requirement that all data in transit must be encrypted. Does Direct Connect alone satisfy that requirement?
options: Yes — Direct Connect is a private connection, so it's encrypted by definition
No — private access control and cryptographic encryption are different guarantees; add a VPN overlay or MACsec
Yes, as long as the virtual interface is configured as public rather than private
No — Direct Connect can never be used for encrypted workloads under any circumstances

scenes.narration: Here's why. Peering connections are a direct routing relationship between exactly two VPCs — Beta has routes to both Alpha and Gamma, but it will never forward one peer's traffic to reach the other. The fix is a direct Alpha-to-Gamma connection, or better, a Transit Gateway both attach to as spokes. And Direct Connect: being a private, dedicated circuit only means nobody outside it can access the medium — it says nothing about whether the bits on that medium are cryptographically protected. They aren't, by default. Satisfying an encryption mandate means adding an IPsec VPN session on top, or MACsec where it's supported — private and encrypted are not the same word.

answers.prompt: Can Alpha reach Gamma through the Alpha–Beta–Gamma peering chain?
answers.correct: No — peering connections are strictly pairwise and never transitive.
answers.rationale: Beta's route table can send Beta's own traffic to Gamma, but it will never forward Alpha's traffic through itself. Reaching Gamma from Alpha needs either a direct Alpha–Gamma peering connection, or replacing the whole design with a Transit Gateway that both attach to as spokes.

answers.prompt: Does Direct Connect alone satisfy an encryption-in-transit requirement?
answers.correct: No — Direct Connect is private by access control, not encrypted by default.
answers.rationale: Nobody outside your dedicated circuit can reach the medium, but that's an access-control property, not a cryptographic one. By default the bits travel in the clear — satisfying the requirement means layering an IPsec VPN session over the private virtual interface, or using MACsec where the port and location support it.

scenes.narration: Five things to carry forward. VPC peering never transits — that chain of assumptions is the exam's favorite trap. Full-mesh peering grows quadratically, N times N minus one over two, while a Transit Gateway hub grows linearly, one attachment per VPC — that gap is the entire justification for the redesign. Direct Connect doesn't encrypt by default; private and encrypted are different guarantees, and a stated encryption requirement means adding a VPN overlay or MACsec. Direct Connect and Site-to-Site VPN are the exam's classic hybrid pair — DX for consistent high-throughput workloads with weeks to spare, VPN for lower-throughput or urgent connectivity that needs to exist in minutes. And Direct Connect Gateway extends one connection's reach across VPCs and regions without touching its throughput ceiling or its encryption gap. Next: chapter eighteen moves from how the network is built to how workloads actually get onto it — the seven Rs of migration strategy and the tooling that executes them.

props.heading: What to remember from this chapter
takeaways: VPC peering is genuinely non-transitive — A peered with B and B peered with C never implies A can reach C, ever.
Full-mesh peering needs N(N−1)/2 connections; Transit Gateway needs N attachments — quadratic versus linear is the whole argument.
Direct Connect does not encrypt by default — pair it with a VPN overlay or MACsec when encryption-in-transit is required.
Direct Connect trades weeks of lead time for consistent throughput; Site-to-Site VPN trades that consistency for minutes-to-hours provisioning and encryption by default.
Direct Connect Gateway extends one connection's reach to multiple VPCs and regions — it never changes that connection's throughput ceiling or encryption gap.
